'''balderdash''' (bâl′dėr-dash), ''n.'' [First in sense 1; of obscure origin, appar. dial. or slang: according to one conjecture, < Dan. ''balder'', noise, clatter (from a verb repr. by Sw. dial. ''ballra'', Norw. ''baldra'', bellow, prattle, = Icel. refl. ''baldrast'', ''ballrast'', clatter; cf. D. LG. ''balderen'', roar, thunder), + ''dash'', repr. Dan. ''daske'', slap, flap: see ''dash''. But the word may be merely one of the numerous popular formations, of no definite elements, so freely made in the Elizabethan period.] '''1†.''' A jumbled mixture of frothy liquors.
{{smaller block|To drink such ''balderdash'' or bonny-clabber.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' Senseless prate; an unmeaning or nonsensical jumble of words; trashy talk or writing.
{{smaller block|I heard him charge this publication with ribaldry, scurrility, billingsgate, and ''balderdash.''
{{right|''Horne Tooke'', Trial, p. 25.}}}}
='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|See ''prattle'', ''n.''}}

'''balderdash''' (bâl′dėr-dash), ''v. t.'' [< ''balderdash'', ''n.''] To jumble and adulterate (liquors); hence, to mix with inferior ingredients; adulterate: with ''with'' before the adulterant: as, to ''balderdash'' wine ''with'' cider. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The wine-merchants of Nice brew and ''balderdash'' and even mix it with pigeon’s dung and quicklime.
{{right|''Smollett'', Travels, xix.}}}}

'''Balder’s-brae''', ''n.'' See ''Balder-brae''.

'''bald-faced''' (bâld′fāst), ''a.'' Having a white face or white on the face: said of animals: as, a ''bald-faced'' stag.

'''baldhead''' (bâld′hed), ''n.'' '''1.''' A man bald on the head. 2 Ki. ii. 23.—'''2.''' The name of a breed of
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''baleful''' (bāl′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''baleful'', ''baluful'', < AS. ''bealufull'', ''bealofull'', < ''bealu'', ''bealo'', bale, + ''-full'', -ful: see ''bale''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ful.''] '''1.''' Full of hurtful or malign influence; destructive; pernicious; noxious; direful; deadly: as, “''baleful'' breath,” ''Dryden;'' “''baleful'' drugs,” ''Milton'', Comus, l. 225.
{{smaller block|<poem>And when he weeps, as you think for his vices,
’Tis but as killing drops from ''baleful'' yew-trees,
That rot their honest neighbour.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iii. 1.}}
This lustful, treacherous, and ''baleful'' woman.
{{right|''Edinburgh Rev.''}}
He reminded him that the ''baleful'' horoscope of Abdallah had predicted the downfall of Granada.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., I. xiv.}}}}
'''2.''' Fraught with bale; full of calamity or misfortune; disastrous; wretched; miserable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah! lucklesse babe, borne under cruel starre,
And in dead parents ''balefull'' ashes bred.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 2.}}
<poem>That ''baleful'' burning night,
When subtle Greeks surpris’d King Priam’s Troy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., v. 3.}}}}

'''balefully''' (bāl′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' [ME. ''balfully'', ''baillfully;'' < ''baleful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a baleful manner. (''a'') Calamitously; perniciously; noxiously. (''b'') Miserably; unhappily; painfully.

'''balefulness''' (bāl′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being baleful.
{{smaller block|Their blisse he turn’d to ''balefulnesse.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 83.}}}}

'''bale-hook''' (bāl′hu̇k), ''n.'' '''1.''' A large hook suspended from the chain of a crane or winch, for use in lifting bales.—'''2.''' A smaller hand-hook
readings.c3s3:
used in handling unwieldy bales, boxes, and packages.

'''baleine''' (ba-lān′), ''n.'' [F., lit. a whale: see ''baleen.''] A movable platform for the support of dumping-wagons, used in France in building railroad embankments.

'''baleis†''', ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''balys'', < ME. ''baleys'', ''baleis'', < OF. ''baleis'', ''balei'', mod. F. ''balai'', a broom, besom, dial. also broom, genesta; cf. Bret. ''balaen'', a broom, besom, ''balan'', broom, genesta.] A rod; a twig.

'''baleless''' (bāl′les), ''a.'' [< ME. ''baleles'', < AS. ''bealuleás'', ''bealoleás'', < ''bealu'', ''bealo'', bale, + ''-leás'', -less: see ''bale''<sup>1</sup> and ''-less.''] Harmless; innocent.

'''baler<sup>1</sup>''' (bā′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''bale''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who bales, or makes up bales or bundles.

'''baler<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''bailer''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bales†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''balas''<sup>1</sup>.

'''balester†''', ''n.'' See ''balister''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bale-tie''' (bāl′tī), ''n.'' A contrivance for joining the ends of the straps used in baling cotton, hay, etc.

'''baliki''' (ba-lē′kē), ''n.'' [Russ.] The back-pieces of the sturgeon, salted and smoked in Russia for home use and exportation.

'''balin†''', ''n.'' [Irreg. < L. ''balin'', acc. of ''balis'', < Gr. βάλλις, an unknown plant: see def.] An unknown plant, supposed to have wonderful medicinal virtues. ''N. E. D.''
{{smaller block|Having th’ herbe ''balin'' in his wounds infus’d.
{{right|''Great Britaines Troy'' (1609).}}}}

{{RunningHeader|balderdash|428|balin}}{{nop}}'''balderdash''' (bâl′dėr-dash), ''n.''   [First in sense 1; of obscure origin, appar. dial. or slang: according to one conjecture, < Dan. ''balder'', noise, clatter (from a verb repr. by Sw. dial. ''ballra'', Norw. ''baldra'', bellow, prattle, = Icel. refl. ''baldrast'', ''ballrast'', clatter; cf. D. LG. ''balderen'', roar, thunder), + ''dash'', repr. Dan. ''daske'', slap, flap: see ''dash''. But the word may be merely one of the numerous popular formations, of no definite elements, so freely made in the Elizabethan period.]   '''1†.''' A jumbled mixture of frothy liquors. {{smaller block|To drink such ''balderdash'' or bonny-clabber. {{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, i. 2.}}}} '''2.''' Senseless prate; an unmeaning or nonsensical jumble of words; trashy talk or writing. {{smaller block|I heard him charge this publication with ribaldry, scurrility, billingsgate, and ''balderdash.'' {{right|''Horne Tooke'', Trial, p. 25.}}}} ='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|See ''prattle'', ''n.''}} '''balderdash''' (bâl′dėr-dash), ''v. t.''   [< ''balderdash'', ''n.'']   To jumble and adulterate (liquors); hence, to mix with inferior ingredients; adulterate: with ''with'' before the adulterant: as, to ''balderdash'' wine ''with'' cider. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The wine-merchants of Nice brew and ''balderdash'' and even mix it with pigeon’s dung and quicklime. {{right|''Smollett'', Travels, xix.}}}} '''Balder’s-brae''', ''n.'' See ''Balder-brae''. '''bald-faced''' (bâld′fāst), ''a.'' Having a white face or white on the face: said of animals: as, a ''bald-faced'' stag. '''baldhead''' (bâld′hed), ''n.'' '''1.''' A man bald on the head. 2 Ki. ii. 23.—'''2.''' The name of a breed of domestic pigeons.—'''3.''' A name of the fruit-crows (''Cotingidæ'') of South America, of the genus ''Gymnocephalus''. ''G. calvus'' is the capuchin baldhead. '''bald-headed''' (bâld′hed″ed), ''a.'' Having a bald head.—{{smaller|'''Bald-headed eagle.''' See ''eagle''.}} '''baldicoot''' (bâl′di-köt), ''n.''   [Also ''baldecoot'', ''baldcoot'', < ''bald''1 + ''coot''; the syllable ''-i-'' is meaningless.]   '''1.''' The common coot, ''Fulica atra''. Hence—'''2.''' Figuratively, a monk, on account of his somber raiment and shaven crown. {{smaller block|Princesses that . . . demean themselves to hob and nob with these black ''baldicoots''. {{right|''Kingsley'', Saint’s Tragedy, iii. 4.}}}} '''baldly''' (bâld′li), ''adv.'' So as to be bald, in any sense of that word. '''baldmoney''' (bâld′mun″i), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''baldimonie'', ''baudmoney'', etc., < ME. ''baldmony'', ''baldemoyn'', ''baldemoyne'', ''baldemoin'', an early name of gentian; origin unknown.]   '''1†.''' A name of various species of gentian.—'''2.''' A name for the mew or spignel, an umbelliferous plant of Europe, ''Meum athamanticum''. '''baldness''' (bâld′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balldnesse''; < ''bald''1 + ''-ness''.]   The state or quality of being bald. {{smaller|(''a'') Lack of hair or natural covering on the head or top; absence or loss of hair. (''b'') Deficiency of appropriate ornament, as in writing; meanness or inelegance; want of ornament: as, ''baldness'' of style.}} {{smaller block|''Baldness'' of allusion and barbarity of versification. {{right|''T. Warton'', Hist. Eng. Poetry, III. 74.}}}} '''baldpate''' (bâld′pāt), ''n.'' '''1.''' A person with a bald head. {{smaller block|Come hither, goodman ''baldpate''. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. i.}}}} 2. In ''ornith.'', a kind of duck with white on the head; a widgeon, ''Mareca penelope'' and ''M. americana.'' See cut under ''widgeon.'' '''baldpate, bald-pated''' (bâld′pāt, -pā″ted), ''a.'' Lacking hair on the pate; shorn of hair. {{smaller block|You ''bald-pated'', lying rascal. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1.}}}} '''baldrib''' (bâld′rib), ''n.'' '''1.''' A joint of pork cut from nearer the rump than the spare-rib, and consisting of a rib from which the fat has been removed. {{smaller block|''Baldrib'', griskin, chine, or chop. {{right|''Southey'', To A. Cunningham.}}}} Hence—'''2.''' Figuratively, a lean, lanky person. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Faith, thou art such a spring ''baldrib'', all the mistresses in the town will never get thee up. {{right|''Middleton.''}}}} '''baldric''' (bâl′drik), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''baudrick'', etc., < ME. ''baudrik'', ''bawdrik'', ''bauderik'', etc., earlier ''baudry'', < OF. ''baudrei'', ''baldrei'', ''baldret'' (later ''baudroy'' and, with added suffix, ''baudrier'') = Pr. ''baudrat'' (ML. ''baldringus''), appar. < MHG. ''balderich'', a girdle, perhaps < OHG. ''balz'' = E. ''belt'', < L. ''balteus'': see ''belt''.]   '''1.''' A belt, or an ornament resembling a belt. {{smaller block|A palmer’s amice wrapt him round, With a wrought Spanish ''baldrick'' bound. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., ii. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|In particular—(''a''†) A belt worn round the waist, as the Roman cingulum, or military belt. (''b'') A jeweled ornament worn round the neck by both ladies and gentlemen in the sixteenth century. ''R. Morris.'' (''c''†) Figuratively, the zodiac. ''Spenser.'' (''d'') A belt worn over the right or left shoulder, crossing the body diagonally to the waist or below it, either simply as an ornament or to suspend a sword, dagger, or horn. Such belts, in medieval and Renaissance times, were sometimes richly decorated and garnished with bells, precious stones, etc.}} {{smaller block|Athwart his brest a ''bauldrick'' brave he ware That shind, like twinkling stars, with stones most pretious rare. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vii. 29.}}}} {{smaller block|And from his blazon’d ''baldric'' slung A mighty silver bugle hung. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lady of Shalott, iii.}}}} '''2†.''' The leather thong or gear by which the clapper of a church-bell was formerly suspended. {{smaller block|In the earliest accounts the ''baldricks'' of the bells are always referred to ''eo nomine'', but later on they are called “leathers.” {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., II. 495.}}}} Also spelled ''baldrick''. '''baldric-wise''' (bâl′drik-wīz), ''adv.''   [< ''baldric'' + ''wise''2.]   After the manner of a baldric; over one shoulder and hanging down to the waist. '''balductum†''', ''n.''   [Also ''balducktum'', < ML. ''balducta'', curd, hot milk curdled with ale or wine, a posset.]   Balderdash; trash. '''Baldwin bit.''' See ''bit''1. '''baldy''' (bâl′di), ''n.''   [< ''bald''1 + dim. ''-y''.]   A nickname for a bald-headed person. [Colloq.] '''bale1''' (bāl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bale'', ''balwe'', ''balw'', ''baluw'', ''balu'', etc., < AS. ''balu'', ''bealu'', ''bealo'' (''bealw-'', ''bealow-'') = OS. ''balu'' = OFries. ''balu-'', ''bale-'' (in comp.) = OHG. ''balo'' = Icel. ''böl'' (not in mod. G. Sw. Dan.), evil, calamity; prop. neut. of the adj. found only in AS. ''balu'', ''bealu'' (''balw-'', ''bealw-'') = MLG. ''bal-'' (in comp.), Goth. ''balws'' (in comp. and deriv.), evil, dire.]   Evil; woe; calamity; misery; that which causes ruin, destruction, or sorrow. [Long obsolete until recently revived in poetry. It occurs especially in alliterative antithesis to ''boot'' or ''bliss''.] {{smaller block|For now this day thou art my ''bale'',
My boote when thou shold bee. {{right|''Robin Hood'', in Percy’s Reliques.}}}} {{smaller block|Yett still he strove to cloke his inward ''bale''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ix. 16.}}}} {{smaller block|Brought hither from their homes to work our ''bale''. {{right|''Southey''.}}}} {{smaller block|A touch, and bliss is turned to ''bale''. {{right|''C. Thaxter'', The Pimpernel.}}}} '''bale2''' (bāl), ''n.''   [Sc. also ''beal'', ''bail''; < ME. ''bale'', ''baile'', ''belle'' (chiefly northern; the reg. southern ME. would be *''bele'', *''bel'', giving mod. E. *''beal'' or *''beel'', like ''deal''1 or ''eel''), < AS. ''bǣl'' = Icel. ''bāl'' = Sw. ''bål'' = Dan. ''baal'', a great fire, a blazing pile, funeral pyre; cf. Skt. ''bhālas'', luster, Gr. φαλός, shining, white: see ''ball''3.]   A large fire built out of doors and burning freely; a bonfire. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A funeral pile or pyre. [Obsolete and poetical.] (''b'') A signal-fire; a beacon. See ''beacon'' and ''bale-fire''.}} {{smaller block|On Penchryst glows a ''bale'' of fire,
And three are kindling on Priesthaughswire. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii. 27.}}}} '''bale3''' (bāl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bale'', < OF. ''bale'', ''balle'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''bala'' = It. ''balla'', < ML. ''bala'', ''balla'', a ball, a round bundle, a package, < OHG. ''balla'', ''palla'', MHG. ''balle'', a ball: see ''ball''1, of which ''bale'' is a doublet.]   '''1.''' A large bundle or package of merchandise prepared for transportation, either in a cloth cover, corded or banded, or without cover, but compressed and secured by transverse bands, wires, or withes and longitudinal slats. {{smaller|The chief articles of merchandise that are baled are cotton, wool, and hay. The weight of a bale of American cotton is between 400 and 500 pounds, varying with the season of production. A bale of cochineal is 1½ hundredweight, a bale of Spanish wool 2¼ hundredweight, a bale of caraway-seeds 3 hundredweight, a bale of Mocha coffee 303 pounds, a bale of thread 100 bolts.}} '''2†.''' A pair or set of dice. {{smaller block|It is a false die of the same ''bale'', but not the same cut. {{right|''Sir T. Overbury'', Characters.}}}} {{smaller block|I have a crew of angels prisoners in my pocket, and none but a good ''bale'' of dice can fetch them out. {{right|''Middleton'', Blurt, Master-Constable, ii.}}}} '''bale3''' (bāl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''baled'', ppr. ''baling''.   [< ''bale''3, ''n.'']   To make up into a bale or bales. '''bale4†, bale5†, bale6†, bale7.''' See ''bail''1, ''bail''2, ''bail''3, ''bail''4. '''Balearian''' (bal-ẹ̄-ā′ri-an), ''a.'' Same as ''Balearic.'' '''Balearic''' (bal-ẹ̄-ar′ik), ''a.''   [< L. ''Balearicus'', better ''Baliaricus'' (Gr. Βαλιαρικός, also Βαλεαρικός and Βαλλιαρικός), < ''Baleares'', better ''Baliares'', Gr. Βαλιαρεῖς, the ancient name of the islands and of their inhabitants, lit., according to the common tradition, the slingers, < Gr. βάλλειν, throw, sling.]   Pertaining to the islands Majorca, Minorca, Iviza, etc., in the Mediterranean sea, called the Balearic islands.—'''Balearic crane.''' {{smaller|See ''Balearica.''}} '''Balearica''' (bal-ẹ̄-ar′i-kạ̈), ''n.''   [NL., fem. sing. of L. ''Balearicus'': see ''Balearic.'']   A genus of cranes, family ''Gruidæ'', including the crowned cranes, ''B. pavonina'' and ''B. regulorum.'' {{smaller|They have a fastigiate fan-shaped erect crest of modified yellowish feathers resembling a miniature wisp-broom. The head is also variegated with black feathers and red naked spaces, and the throat is wattled; the general plumage is blackish, with much white on the wings. The total length is about 4 feet. These cranes occur in various parts of Africa, as well as in the islands to which they owe their name, and one species has occasionally been found in Europe. The genus has also been named ''Balearius'' (Rafinesque, 1815) and ''Geranarchus'' (Gloger, 1842).}} '''balearican''' (bal-ẹ̄-ar′i-kan), ''n.''   [< ''Balearica.'']   A crane of the genus ''Balearica.'' '''baleen''' (ba-lēn′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balene'', ''baleyne'', a whale, < OF. ''balene'', F. ''baleine'', < L. ''balæna'', a whale: see ''Balæna.'']   '''1†.''' A whale.—'''2†.''' The sea-bream.—'''3.''' Whalebone in its natural state: a name given by whale-fishers. {{smaller block|The horny “teeth” of the Lampreys, and of Ornithorhynchus, appear to be ecderonic structures, homologous with the ''baleen'' of the Cetacea, with the palatal plates of the Sirenia, or the beaks of Birds and Reptiles, and not with true teeth. {{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 80.}}}} '''baleen-knife''' (ba-lēn′nīf), ''n.'' A double-handled knife with a curved blade, used for splitting whalebone. '''bale-fire''' (bāl′fīr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balefyre'', < AS. ''bǣlfȳr'', < ''bǣl'', bale, + ''fȳr'', fire: see ''bale''2 and ''fire.'']   '''1.''' A large fire in the open air; particularly, the fire of a funeral pile. {{smaller block|The festival [of the death of the earth in winter] was . . . kept by the lighting of great fires, called ''bale-fires.'' {{right|''Keary'', Prim. Belief, p. 227.}}}} '''2.''' A beacon- or signal-fire. {{smaller block|Sweet Teviot! on thy silver tide The glaring ''bale-fires'' blaze no more. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iv. 1.}}}} '''baleful''' (bāl′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''baleful'', ''baluful'', < AS. ''bealufull'', ''bealofull'', < ''bealu'', ''bealo'', bale, + ''-full'', -ful: see ''bale''1 and ''-ful.'']   '''1.''' Full of hurtful or malign influence; destructive; pernicious; noxious; direful; deadly: as, “''baleful'' breath,” ''Dryden;'' “''baleful'' drugs,” ''Milton'', Comus, l. 225. {{smaller block|And when he weeps, as you think for his vices, ’Tis but as killing drops from ''baleful'' yew-trees, That rot their honest neighbour. {{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|This lustful, treacherous, and ''baleful'' woman. {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.''}}}} {{smaller block|He reminded him that the ''baleful'' horoscope of Abdallah had predicted the downfall of Granada. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., I. xiv.}}}} '''2.''' Fraught with bale; full of calamity or misfortune; disastrous; wretched; miserable. {{smaller block|Ah! lucklesse babe, borne under cruel starre, And in dead parents ''balefull'' ashes bred. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|That ''baleful'' burning night, When subtle Greeks surpris’d King Priam’s Troy. {{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., v. 3.}}}} '''balefully''' (bāl′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [ME. ''balfully'', ''baillfully;'' < ''baleful'' + ''-ly''2.]   In a baleful manner. (''a'') Calamitously; perniciously; noxiously. (''b'') Miserably; unhappily; painfully. '''balefulness''' (bāl′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being baleful. {{smaller block|Their blisse he turn’d to ''balefulnesse.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 83.}}}} '''bale-hook''' (bāl′hu̇k), ''n.'' '''1.''' A large hook suspended from the chain of a crane or winch, for use in lifting bales.—'''2.''' A smaller hand-hook used in handling unwieldy bales, boxes, and packages. '''baleine''' (ba-lān′), ''n.''   [F., lit. a whale: see ''baleen.'']   A movable platform for the support of dumping-wagons, used in France in building railroad embankments. '''baleis†''', ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''balys'', < ME. ''baleys'', ''baleis'', < OF. ''baleis'', ''balei'', mod. F. ''balai'', a broom, besom, dial. also broom, genesta; cf. Bret. ''balaen'', a broom, besom, ''balan'', broom, genesta.]   A rod; a twig. '''baleless''' (bāl′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''baleles'', < AS. ''bealuleás'', ''bealoleás'', < ''bealu'', ''bealo'', bale, + ''-leás'', -less: see ''bale''1 and ''-less.'']   Harmless; innocent. '''baler1''' (bā′lėr), ''n.''   [< ''bale''3, ''v.'', + ''-er''1.]   One who bales, or makes up bales or bundles. '''baler2''', ''n.'' See ''bailer''2. '''bales†''', ''n.''
